content.title: A Multi-Stage Dockerfile for a Go Service
content.text:
A Go binary is statically linked and self-contained, which makes it a perfect candidate for a tiny container image. Yet the first Dockerfile most people write for a Go service ships the entire toolchain, the module cache, and the source tree alongside a binary that needs none of them. This walkthrough starts from that naive image, moves to a two-stage build with a distroless final image, and measures the difference.

The service is a small HTTP API with its main package at ./cmd/api. The single-stage Dockerfile people usually start with looks like this:

FROM golang:1.23
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app ./cmd/api
CMD ["/app"]

Build it with docker build -t api:naive . and check docker images. On my machine the result is 1.14 GB. Nearly all of that is the golang base image, compilers, and the module download cache. None of it runs in production, and all of it is attack surface and pull time.

The fix is to build in one stage and copy only the binary into a second, minimal stage. Replace the Dockerfile with:

FROM golang:1.23 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=builder /out/api /api
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

Each choice in the builder stage has a reason. Copying go.mod and go.sum first and running go mod download before copying the rest means the dependency layer is cached until those two files change, so a source edit does not trigger a full re-download. CGO_ENABLED=0 forces a fully static binary with no dependency on a C library, which is what allows the final image to contain nothing but the binary. The -trimpath flag strips local filesystem paths from the binary, and -s -w drops the symbol table and debug information, which typically cuts the binary size by a quarter to a third. If you rely on stack traces with file paths, leave -trimpath out.

The final stage uses the static variant of distroless. It contains a CA certificate bundle, a timezone database, a minimal /etc/passwd, and nothing else: no shell, no package manager, no libc. The nonroot tag runs the process as UID 65532 by default, and the explicit USER line makes that intent visible. If your binary needs to make outbound HTTPS calls, the certificate bundle in this image is exactly what makes them work; if you used scratch instead, you would have to copy certificates in yourself.

Build the new image with docker build -t api:multistage . and compare:

docker images api

api   naive        1.14GB
api   multistage   12.3MB

About 10 MB of that is the binary and 2 MB is the distroless base. The image pulls in a couple of seconds and there is nothing inside to exploit beyond your own code.

One more file matters. Without a .dockerignore, COPY . . sends your entire working directory to the build daemon, including the .git history, local build outputs, and any .env files sitting around. Create .dockerignore next to the Dockerfile:

.git
.gitignore
*.md
bin/
dist/
.env
.env.*
Dockerfile
.dockerignore

This speeds up the build context transfer and, more importantly, keeps secrets and history out of intermediate layers where they can be recovered with docker history or by inspecting the builder stage.

Two debugging notes for the distroless image. Because there is no shell, docker exec -it container sh will fail. To inspect a running container use docker debug if your Docker version has it, or temporarily switch the final stage to gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:debug, which adds a busybox shell. Never ship the debug tag to production. Second, if the container exits immediately with a message about no such file or directory even though the binary is clearly present, you almost certainly forgot CGO_ENABLED=0 and the binary is looking for a dynamic loader that does not exist in the image. Rebuild with the flag and the problem disappears.

Run the result with docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 api:multistage and hit the endpoint. Same service, one percent of the image, and a much smaller thing to worry about.

notes: Standard multi-stage Docker tutorial with correct flags, concrete size numbers, and a .dockerignore. A correct judge should score it as practically useful and accurate but well-trodden ground for anyone who has containerised Go before.
